verified.title: Retry withdraws staged change and fails waiting step before its attempt-ceiling check can refuse
verified.boundary: manager.server.ts retry(): the round-3 claim that Retry validates first holds only for the envelope check. The attempt-ceiling refusal runs after promotion-waiting steps are failed and their staged changes withdrawn.
verified.reproduction: Code-path trace, not executed. A device-attributed filesystem.write stages on a step whose attempt count is at the ceiling boundary. Retry admits a failed step with attempts.length <= 2*maxRetriesPerStep+1 (the check uses '>'). Running it adds an attempt via markRunning, so the step waits for promotion with attempts.length = 2*maxRetriesPerStep+2. The workstation then calls Retry on the failed mission. Line 4324 sets the waiting step to failed with detail 'the change is staged again for a fresh review'. Line 4325 withdraws its STAGED record and denies the open promotion request. The loop at 4331-4336 then throws 'reached its attempt ceiling; replan instead'. The mission stays failed.
verified.evidence: src/lib/bunny-missions/manager.server.ts:4322-4337 (first loop, withdrawStaged, failed-list, ceiling throw). Line 4324 is the false detail text, 4325 the withdrawal, 4333-4334 the throw after mutation. Attempts grow per run in markRunning at line 1275. The mission is not stranded, but the staged change is destroyed and the step reports a retry that was refused.
verified.repair: Run every refusal check (attempt ceiling, no-failed-step) over all failed and promotion-waiting steps before any setStep or withdrawStaged call, then apply the reset and withdrawal. Or wrap the whole Retry in one transaction. Never describe a refused Retry as staged again.

votes.reasoning: The finding is real on the code path, and it is not documented intent. Retry (manager.server.ts:4319-4337) runs the promotion-waiting loop (4322-4324) and withdrawStaged (4325) before the attempt-ceiling check inside the failed-steps loop (4331-4334). Those earlier mutations are not wrapped in a transaction, so they persist when the ceiling throw fires. The reachability holds: the ceiling check uses '>' (4332), so a failed step with attempts.length == 2*maxRetries+1 is admitted, and markRunning (1268-1275) adds one attempt when it runs, giving 2*maxRetries+2 while it waits for promotion. The next Retry then fails that step, and endStaged (2578-2588) sets the record WITHDRAWN and denies the open request. The throw follows, so the staged change is destroyed and the step keeps the false detail "the change is staged again for a fresh review". No promotion happens and no ceiling is loosened, so there is no authority impact. Subsequent Retries stay refused, so the step is stuck until a replan. Severity is LOW rather than MEDIUM: the failure is fail-closed and the lost content is recoverable by rerunning the task. I did not execute a probe; this rests on the code trace.

Confirmed by reading the working tree (manager.server.ts retry(), lines ~4318-4337 as printed). Sequence: (1) the promotion-waiting loop sets each waiting_for_approval step with a pending promotion request to state "failed" with detail "the change is staged again for a fresh review"; (2) withdrawStaged(id, ...) runs for the whole mission, discarding staged changes and denying open promotion requests; (3) `steps` is re-read and `failed` is filtered, so the just-failed waiting step is included; (4) the attempt-ceiling check `step.attempts.length > step.maxRetries * 2 + 1` throws "reached its attempt ceiling; replan instead" before setMission(... "ready") runs, so the mission stays failed. The mutations in steps 1-2 are persisted before the throw, and there is no rollback. The ceiling is reachable: a failed step at attempts.length 2*max+1 is admitted by Retry, markRunning (attempts+1) makes it 2*max+2 while waiting for promotion, and a second Retry hits this path. The round-3 claim "Retry validates first" therefore holds only for the envelope check. Caveats for severity: no authority impact (the change is withdrawn, not applied, and the mission stays failed and safe), so the impact is loss of staged work plus a false detail string. I would rate it LOW-to-MEDIUM rather than HIGH. I did not execute a probe; the verdict rests on code-path reading, which is what the finding itself describes.
votes.severityIfReal: MEDIUM (arguably LOW: no authority impact, but staged work is destroyed and the step reports a false retry message)

verified.title: Agent-instruction @-imports of docs files classify as PHONE_SAFE_DOCUMENT
verified.boundary: classifyDeviceWrite on a Markdown destination that a root agent-instruction file imports. Only PROJECT_MANIFESTS and .github/workflows are scanned for mentions; CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and similar root instruction files are never scanned.
verified.reproduction: Project root has CLAUDE.md containing the line '@docs/rules.md'. Remote envelope write (or overwrite:true on an existing docs/rules.md) of path 'docs/rules.md' with plain Markdown content. classifyDeviceWrite returns PHONE_SAFE_DOCUMENT ('plain document'), so deviceWriteClassRefusal allows it and the device write is staged with a phone-safe classification. Claude Code loads @-imported files from CLAUDE.md as agent instructions, so the device controls agent instructions.
verified.evidence: Probe run: CLAUDE.md='@docs/rules.md' fixture, classify 'docs/rules.md' -> PHONE_SAFE_DOCUMENT. Code: authorization.server.ts:533 PROJECT_MANIFESTS omits CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md/GEMINI.md; mentionedByManifests at :546-560 only reads that list and .github/workflows; the agent-file leaf regex at :524 only matches the instruction file's own name, not what it imports; check at :624.
verified.repair: Add every root agent-instruction file (CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, AGENTS.md, GEMINI.md, QWEN.md, .github/copilot-instructions.md, .clinerules, .cursorrules, .windsurfrules, .mcp.json) to the mention scan, and classify any file they reference as AGENT_INSTRUCTIONS.

votes.reasoning:
The classification gap is real, but the HIGH severity and "device controls agent instructions" wording are overstated.

Confirmed in code (read-only, no probe run):
- authorization.server.ts:533 PROJECT_MANIFESTS lists package.json, Makefile, tsconfig, vite config, Dockerfile, etc. It omits CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and GEMINI.md.
- authorization.server.ts:546-560 mentionedByManifests reads only PROJECT_MANIFESTS and .github/workflows, so an @-import in a root instruction file is never seen.
- For 'docs/rules.md' the leaf is 'rules.md'. It does not match AGENT_INSTRUCTION_FILE, and 'docs' is in DATA_DIR, not AGENT_INSTRUCTION_DIR. It is not a program start, has no ESM import/export line in plain Markdown, and does not exist as a program. It therefore falls through to PHONE_SAFE_DOCUMENT (authorization.server.ts:624-626).
- deviceWriteClassRefusal (authorization.server.ts:642-645) then returns null, so the device write is allowed to stage.

Why the impact is bounded:
- Every staged paired-device change still requires promotion on the Windows Host. manager.server.ts:2560 raises a filesystem.promote permission request, and promoteStaged (manager.server.ts:2615) runs only on host approval. Nothing reaches the project without that approval.
- The host review text includes the classification and its reason (manager.server.ts:2556), and the warning says any program can read the file. The reviewer sees "PHONE_SAFE_DOCUMENT / plain document", which is a misleading label for a file an agent imports.

So the real defect is that the D1 contract ("only PHONE_SAFE classes receive phone-write authority"; AGENT_INSTRUCTIONS needs the Host) is not enforced for @-imported instruction files. The device can stage a change to content that Claude Code loads as instructions, and the review label understates it. The gate is still the Host promotion. I rate this MEDIUM, not HIGH.

The classifier gap is real, confirmed by reading the working tree (no probe re-run). In src/lib/bunny-missions/authorization.server.ts, PROJECT_MANIFESTS (line ~533) lists no CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md or GEMINI.md, and mentionedByManifests (546-560) only scans that list plus .github/workflows. For destination docs/rules.md, the leaf and directory names match no AGENT_INSTRUCTION pattern (the docs directory is only in DATA_DIR, which applies to structured data). Nothing in the chain reads a root CLAUDE.md's @-imports, so the write falls through to the DOCUMENT_FILE branch at line ~637 and returns PHONE_SAFE_DOCUMENT. deviceWriteClassRefusal (line ~644) then allows it, so a device can stage the write. This is a real gap in the classification layer and it does grant a device a stageable path it should be refused. It is not as severe as stated. Staging is inert (staging.server.ts header: content lives in private Host state, is never executed or listed), and bytes move into the project only on a workstation promotion answer (manager.server.ts ~2636-2706). The host reviewer is the actual gate, and I did not verify that the promotion review surfaces the PHONE_SAFE classification or the @-import relationship. The claim "the device controls agent instructions" therefore overstates the impact: it depends on a host operator approving. Because the gap has some authority impact, I do not refute it outright. I downgrade it to MEDIUM.

A remote write (overwrite:true for an existing docs/ci.yml, or a new file) of 'docs/ci.yml' with 'stages: [x]' classifies PHONE_SAFE_DATA ('JSON or YAML inside a recognized data or document folder'). GitLab CI evaluates included local YAML job definitions, including script: entries, when the pipeline runs after push.
verified.evidence: Probe run: .gitlab-ci.yml fixture with 'local: docs/ci.yml' -> classify 'docs/ci.yml' = PHONE_SAFE_DATA. Code: authorization.server.ts:533 (PROJECT_MANIFESTS lacks CI files), :546-560 (mention scan), :627-630 (structured data in DATA_DIR -> PHONE_SAFE_DATA).

Also treat YAML/JSON as CONFIGURATION when its name matches a known CI or tool config name, whatever folder it sits in.

votes.reasoning: The misclassification is real. A standalone copy of classifyDeviceWrite (lines 121-150 and 510-645 of src/lib/bunny-missions/authorization.server.ts, run under bun from scratchpad/review-probes/r4/skeptic-classifier-0/) classifies docs/ci.yml as PHONE_SAFE_DATA with a root .gitlab-ci.yml containing "include: - local: docs/ci.yml" present. The probe's reasons show only "JSON or YAML inside a recognized data or document folder". mentionedByManifests (authorization.server.ts:546-560) scans only PROJECT_MANIFESTS (line 533, which has no .gitlab-ci.yml, Jenkinsfile, azure-pipelines.yml or buildspec.yml) and .github/workflows, so the include is never seen. This is not documented intended behavior. The contract lists .gitlab only as an execution folder, and the mention check is meant to catch files named as tool inputs. The HIGH rating is overstated, though. Every device write is staged inertly (manager.server.ts:2522-2540, contract lines 27-36), and promotion into the project always requires a workstation allow_once on a desktopRequired filesystem.promote request (contract lines 36-42). A PHONE_SAFE label therefore does not let a phone execute or land content without host approval. Its effects are narrower: the host reviewer sees a PHONE_SAFE_DATA label and a generic warning instead of EXECUTION_RELEVANT, and under a remote envelope the write skips the desktopRequired ask that a non-safe class would get. That is a real labeling and gating gap, worth fixing by adding the root CI filenames to the mention scan or treating CI-named YAML as execution-relevant, but not a bypass of the workstation gate.

The gap is real, confirmed by static trace of classifyDeviceWrite (authorization.server.ts:533, 546-560, 595-630). For docs/ci.yml with a root .gitlab-ci.yml including it: no 8.3 name, no link, no agent-instruction/execution/watched dir match; the leaf ci.yml does not match EXECUTION_CONFIG_FILE (which lists .gitlab-ci.yml only as a leaf, line 123); docs is in DATA_DIR; mentionedByManifests scans only PROJECT_MANIFESTS (no CI files) and .github/workflows (line 555-558), so the include is never seen; the structured-data branch (627-629) returns PHONE_SAFE_DATA. A paired device can therefore initiate a write that GitLab CI would evaluate. Mitigating factors: device writes are staged (D2) and promoted only after Windows Host decision/inspection (staging.server.ts decidedBy/inspectedHash), so a host reviewer is the actual gate; the classifier is documented as risk reduction. The finding's framing of HIGH is arguable because the host review gate remains, but the classification itself grants phone-initiated authority over a file CI executes, which contradicts the stated "devices never authorize code execution" invariant. I did not run a runtime probe: bun failed to load the module (node:sqlite built-in missing), so the evidence is code-trace only. Suggested severity MEDIUM to HIGH; I would rate it MEDIUM given the host gate.

votes.reasoning: Confirmed real. authorization.server.ts:546-556 builds needle from the relative path (backslashes to slashes, lowercased) and tests plain includes() against manifest text where only backslashes are normalized. The finding reproduces against the working tree (probe: /c/Users/allam/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/C--Users-allam-Documents-new-bun-router/133abb7b-876a-4654-a1f2-ee186fd14586/scratchpad/review-probes/r4/skeptic-classifier-1/r4-manifest-spelling.mts, run with node 24 --experimental-strip-types against src/lib/bunny-missions/authorization.server.ts). verified.title: Manifests over 256 KiB are silently skipped, so their references are not seen
verified.boundary: mentionedByManifests returns false for any manifest larger than MANIFEST_READ_LIMIT, so a fail-open skip hides every reference in that file.
verified.reproduction: Root package.json padded to about 300 KiB with a script that reads 'docs/bigcfg.json'. A remote write of 'docs/bigcfg.json' classifies PHONE_SAFE_DATA. The same file under 256 KiB classifies EXECUTION_RELEVANT.
verified.evidence: Probe: package.json of 307,250 bytes containing 'docs/bigcfg.json' -> PHONE_SAFE_DATA. Code: authorization.server.ts:534 (limit), :552 (size check returns false, not unknown).
verified.repair: Fail closed: an oversize, unreadable or non-regular manifest means the destination is UNKNOWN, or read the whole file in bounded chunks instead of skipping it.

votes.reasoning: Not refuted: the mechanism is real in the working tree. authorization.server.ts:534 sets MANIFEST_READ_LIMIT = 256 KiB. At :552 the mentions() helper returns false when info.size > MANIFEST_READ_LIMIT, and the catch at :553 also returns false. So an oversize manifest is treated as "no mention" rather than UNKNOWN or EXECUTION_RELEVANT. The caller at :624-625 then skips the manifest-reference rule, and a write to a data file named inside that manifest can fall through to PHONE_SAFE_DATA at :629/:633. The code comment at :532 describes the manifests as the tool-input check, and nothing in the source documents the size skip as intended behavior, so this is a fail-open gap. I did not execute the 307 KB probe; the finding rests on code reading of :552, which is unambiguous. Mitigating factors that lower the severity: a manifest over 256 KiB must already exist in the project because a paired device cannot write package.json (CONFIGURATION, per :608/:615), and classified writes are staged for Windows Host review before promotion (manager.server.ts:2522, :2669). The promotion-time reclassification uses the same function, so it does not catch this gap either; the human review gate is the real backstop. Overlap with the documented "data read by arbitrary project scripts" limitation is partial: this gap is a specific classifier fail-open that the classifier's own manifest rule was meant to close. The same fail-open also applies to unreadable manifests (the catch at :553), which is a sibling of the reported bug and worth noting.
votes.severityIfReal: LOW (reported MEDIUM): real fail-open, but the precondition is a pre-existing >256 KiB manifest and staged writes get Windows Host review. Sibling: the readFileSync catch at :553 is also fail-open.

votes.reasoning:
The finding reproduces against the working tree. Probe (node 24 type stripping, importing src/lib/bunny-missions/authorization.server.ts via file URL) with a root package.json whose script reads docs/bigcfg.json: at 1,000 bytes the write to docs/bigcfg.json classifies EXECUTION_RELEVANT ("named by project metadata (package.json) as a tool input"); at 300,091 bytes it classifies PHONE_SAFE_DATA ("JSON or YAML inside a recognized data or document folder"). Code: authorization.server.ts:534 sets MANIFEST_READ_LIMIT = 256 KiB; mentions() at :552 is `info.isFile() && info.size <= MANIFEST_READ_LIMIT && ...`, so an oversize manifest yields false (not-mentioned) rather than unknown or execution-relevant, and the catch at :553 also returns false. This is a real fail-open in a security classifier, not documented behavior: the documented limitation covers data read by arbitrary scripts, not a designed manifest check being silently switched off. Mitigating factors that argue against a higher rating: the attacker must already have a manifest over 256 KiB in the project (a phone cannot write manifests, which are EXECUTION_RELEVANT/CONFIGURATION), and any phone write still goes through Windows-host staging review (D2). Severity therefore sits at MEDIUM at most, arguably LOW, but the defect is reproducible. Probe artifacts are under scratchpad/review-probes/r4/skeptic-classifier-1/ (sk1-out.txt, sk1-out2.txt, probe2.ts); no repository files were edited.</reasoning>
<parameter name="severityIfReal">MEDIUM

verified.title: Subdirectory package manifests and configs are never scanned
verified.boundary: mentionedByManifests only reads manifests directly under the classification root. Monorepo packages keep their own package.json, tsconfig and tool configs in subfolders.
verified.reproduction: apps/web/package.json contains a script that reads 'data/sub.json' relative to apps/web. A remote write of 'apps/web/data/sub.json' classifies PHONE_SAFE_DATA, although a tool run from apps/web reads it as configuration.
verified.evidence: Probe: apps/web/package.json referencing 'data/sub.json' -> classify 'apps/web/data/sub.json' = PHONE_SAFE_DATA. Code: authorization.server.ts:546-550 (manifests resolved only against root).
verified.repair: Scan every manifest or config file within the write's ancestor folders (from the root down to the destination's folder), and resolve each reference relative to that manifest's own folder.

Mitigating factors: the classifier is documented as risk reduction, and device writes go through inert staging (D2) reviewed on the Windows Host before promotion, so the impact is bounded to the review gate and a phone-writable data file that a monorepo tool reads as settings. Tool-config leaf names (e.g. vite.config.ts) are still caught by leaf checks, so the gap is specifically content-based manifest references below root. The behavior reproduces. Under Node 24 with type stripping (probe at scratchpad/review-probes/r4/skeptic-classifier-1/probe.mjs, fixture proj/apps/web/package.json referencing data/sub.json), classifyDeviceWrite("apps/web/data/sub.json") returns PHONE_SAFE_DATA with the warning "Programs may read..." style note. But the finding's own repro would not be caught even if they were scanned, because the needle is the root-relative path "apps/web/data/sub.json" while the script text says "data/sub.json". Also, the claim that subfolder tsconfig and tool configs are never scanned is inaccurate: EXECUTION_CONFIG_FILE (line 123) matches by leaf name at any depth, so apps/web/package.json, tsconfig*.json and similar files classify as CONFIGURATION. The only real gap is a data file in a subfolder read by a script whose name lives in a subfolder manifest. That is the documented limitation "data files read by arbitrary project scripts", which the review explicitly excludes, and the classifier already attaches a warning that programs may read structured data. No new authority is granted beyond that accepted limitation, so this should not be reported as a separate MEDIUM finding.

verified.title: docs/_config.yml (Jekyll/GitHub Pages site config) classifies as PHONE_SAFE_DATA
verified.boundary: Structured data in a DATA_DIR folder is PHONE_SAFE_DATA. A Jekyll _config.yml in docs/ (the GitHub Pages /docs source) configures the site build: plugins, plugins_dir, exclude and safe settings.
verified.reproduction: Remote write of 'docs/_config.yml' with 'plugins_dir: ../scripts' (or 'plugins: [...]') classifies PHONE_SAFE_DATA. Jekyll and GitHub Pages read _config.yml in the source folder, so the content configures the build. The same file at project root correctly classifies CONFIGURATION.
verified.evidence: Probe: 'docs/_config.yml' -> PHONE_SAFE_DATA ('JSON or YAML inside a recognized data or document folder'). Code: authorization.server.ts:627-630, CONFIG_DIR and CONSUMED lists at :529-531 do not mention _config.yml, and it is not a dotfile.
verified.repair: Treat any file named _config.yml, _config.yaml or config.* as CONFIGURATION in every folder, not only at the root. Add Jekyll, Hugo, MkDocs and VitePress site-config names to EXECUTION_CONFIG_FILE.

votes.reasoning: Classification is real but has no authority impact, and it is intended behavior. Trace of classifyDeviceWrite for "docs/_config.yml" (authorization.server.ts:568-640): the leaf is not an agent-instruction, Git, hook, watched-source, or EXECUTION_CONFIG_FILE match (that regex at line 123 has no _config entry); dirs=["docs"] matches DATA_DIR (line 592 regex, which includes docs) and not CONFIG_DIR; the leaf is not a dotfile and not CONSUMED_TEXT_FILE; there is no program-start or ESM content; manifests do not name it. The STRUCTURED_DATA_FILE branch (line 627-630) therefore returns PHONE_SAFE_DATA with a warning "Structured data can still be read by programs as settings; review its consumers." I did not execute a probe; this is from reading the code. The finding's premise that _config.yml configures a build is correct, but the phone-write classes never grant execution or promotion. Every device write is staged unconditionally (manager.server.ts:2522-2540), and the change reaches the project only after Windows Host review and promotion, so the classification changes only whether the write is refused outright. The consequence is that a Host reviewer sees a PHONE_SAFE_DATA label and the warning rather than an EXECUTION_RELEVANT label. That is a review-quality concern, not a reproducible bypass. It also falls under the documented risk-reduction framing of the classifier (line 565-567 comment: "risk reduction, never a proof"). Nothing in the contract is violated.

Not refuted: the misclassification is real, but its authority impact is smaller than MEDIUM. Code trace (not executed; my bun/node probe could not load authorization.server.ts because of node:sqlite and file-URL issues): authorization.server.ts:123 EXECUTION_CONFIG_FILE has no _config.yml entry, so the leaf passes the config checks at :610-626. GIT/dotfile/CONFIG_DIR/CONSUMED checks do not match 'docs' or '_config.yml'. Line 627-630: STRUCTURED_DATA_FILE matches, and 'docs' matches DATA_DIR (:/^(data|...|docs|...)$/), so PHONE_SAFE_DATA is returned. The same path at project root goes to CONFIGURATION, so the gap is a real inconsistency with the classifier's own stated rule ('file or folder that configures programs that run'). Mitigations that reduce authority impact: device-attributed writes are never applied to the project directly; manager.server.ts:2503-2528 routes them into Host-owned inert staging and promotion requires Windows-side review. The classifier also attaches the warning 'Structured data can still be read by programs as settings; review its consumers.' (authorization.server.ts:628) to the result. The repo's docs/ currently has no _config.yml, and a Jekyll/GitHub Pages build config is only consulted when someone runs the build. So a phone can propose a Jekyll config change that reaches the Host reviewer labelled PHONE_SAFE_DATA, where a non-safe class would have been refused outright at authorization.server.ts:250. The same gap likely covers other YAML build configs in data folders (e.g. mkdocs.yml, whose hooks run Python), which would make the class broader but still reviewer-gated. Severity revised to LOW for the reviewed case. Refuted=false because the misclassification is demonstrable in code, not intended behavior.</reasoning>
<parameter name="severityIfReal">LOW

verified.title: Requirements files with a non-standard prefix classify as PHONE_SAFE_DOCUMENT
verified.boundary: CONSUMED_TEXT_FILE is anchored to a leading 'requirements' or 'constraints' prefix, so dev-requirements.txt, test-requirements.txt and similar pip input files pass as plain documents.
verified.reproduction: Remote write of 'dev-requirements.txt' with '-e ./tools' (or a '--index-url' line) classifies PHONE_SAFE_DOCUMENT. pip install -r reads it: '-e ./path' runs that package's setup.py during install, and '--index-url' redirects the package source. Whether a tool runs it depends on the project's CI or scripts, which the mention scan does not check for this file.
verified.evidence: Probe: 'dev-requirements.txt' -> PHONE_SAFE_DOCUMENT ('plain document'). Code: authorization.server.ts:531 (CONSUMED_TEXT_FILE anchored with ^requirements), :615 check.
verified.repair: Match requirements-style names anywhere in the file name (e.g. /requirements|constraints/i with .txt) or classify every .txt whose content contains pip directives (-r, -e, --index-url, --find-links) as EXECUTION_RELEVANT.

votes.reasoning: Not refuted. The gap is real at the regex level and nothing else in classifyDeviceWrite catches the name. authorization.server.ts:531 anchors CONSUMED_TEXT_FILE to ^requirements or ^constraints, so dev-requirements.txt, test-requirements.txt and prod-constraints.txt fail it. A probe of the same regex (scratchpad/review-probes/r4/skeptic-classifier-0/regex-probe.mjs) confirmed: dev-requirements.txt consumed=false document=true, test-requirements.txt consumed=false, prod-constraints.txt consumed=false, while requirements-dev.txt and requirements.txt match. For a root-level file with no dir segments, the only remaining gates are the content check (startsLikeProgram, which "-e ./tools" does not trip), the existing-content check (none for a new file), and mentionedByManifests (only true if a listed manifest or workflow names the path). So the file falls through to the PHONE_SAFE_DOCUMENT return at line 637. Not a documented-intent case: the list is explicitly for package-manager inputs, and the prefix anchor is an omission, not a stated limitation. Caveat: I could not run the full classifier because bun 1.3.14 lacks node:sqlite, which the module imports, so the end-to-end result is from code reading plus the regex probe. Mitigation that keeps this at MEDIUM: phone writes are staged and reviewed on the Windows Host before promotion (the warning at line 636 says so), so a human sees "-e ./tools" or "--index-url" before it reaches the project. The residual risk is that the classification label grants phone write authority to a file pip executes at install time. Suggested fix: anchor the consumed-file rule to the basename pattern (e.g. (^|[-_.])(requirements|constraints)[\w.-]*\.txt$), and add the same check to mentionedByManifests-style scanning if desired.

Probe under scratchpad/review-probes/r4/skeptic-classifier-1/ (probe.ts plus authz-probe.ts, a copy of authorization.server.ts with runtime imports stubbed; bun cannot load the real module because of node:sqlite) reproduces the claim. classifyDeviceWrite on a project base returns: dev-requirements.txt with "-e ./tools" and "--index-url" content -> PHONE_SAFE_DOCUMENT ("plain document"); requirements/base.txt -> PHONE_SAFE_DOCUMENT (the dir "requirements" is in no list); requirements.txt -> CONFIGURATION (the anchored CONSUMED_TEXT_FILE regex matches only the exact prefix). low.title: endDeviceAnswers reports already-consumed one-time answers as invalidated
low.boundary: Device revocation or sign-out while a device-answered one-time grant is already CONSUMED but still attached to a running or verifying step. Provenance and audit only; the lifecycle stamp itself stays correct.
low.reproduction: Device answers a filesystem.write ask on a capability step; the write is admitted (onceAdmitted stamps CONSUMED); the step is still verifying so step.approvedOnce is still set. Then the device signs out or is revoked. endDeviceAnswers finds the step, clears approvedOnce, calls stampLifecycle (which silently returns false because lifecycle already exists), but still emits approval.device_revoked saying the one-time answer 'no longer applies' and increments the returned count that device.revoke reports as unused one-time answer(s).
low.evidence: src/lib/bunny-missions/manager.server.ts ~2448-2455 (stampLifecycle return value ignored; emit and ended++ unconditional); stampLifecycle ~2462-2468 returns false on existing lifecycle; src/lib/bunny-host/http.server.ts ~842 and ~752 (count reported as 'unused one-time answer(s)'). Status: traced from code, not executed.
low.repair: Only emit the approval.device_revoked event and increment the count when stampLifecycle returns true (or when the lifecycle state read back is the one being applied). Otherwise record that the answer was already consumed.

verified.title: Skill-step one-time grant is reused by a re-run after allow_batch (CONSUMED grant revives)
verified.boundary: Plain (non-Agent) Mission, workstation-answered one-time filesystem.write on a step whose executor is a skill. Device answers cannot reach this path (manager.server.ts:2135 refuses device answers on skill steps), so the trigger is workstation-only. Affects the one-time-grant invariant: at most one admitted execution per grant within the step's execution+verification scope.
verified.reproduction: 1) Mission with a skill step (e.g. steps: filesystem.write then terminal.exec). 2) Workstation allow_once on the filesystem.write ask: step.approvedOnce = W (action filesystem.write). 3) Skill run admits the write under oneTime; bus.onceAdmitted stamps W CONSUMED (capabilities/bus.server.ts:318) but does not clear step.approvedOnce. 4) The skill's terminal.exec step asks; askPermission (manager.server.ts ~3870-3880) sets waiting_for_approval without clearing approvedOnce. 5) Workstation answers allow_batch on the terminal.exec offer: respond() calls setStep(step,{state:'ready',pendingRequestId:null,pendingPhase:null}) (manager.server.ts ~4102-4106), which leaves approvedOnce = W. 6) runDeterministic's skill branch builds skills.run options with oneTimeAction: step.approvedOnce?.action (manager.server.ts ~1655) and never calls liveOnce (liveOnce is called only in capabilityRequest, manager.server.ts ~1560). 7) The re-run's filesystem.write is admitted via decide(oneTime) (bus.server.ts:187) with no approval, although W was already CONSUMED.
verified.evidence: src/lib/bunny-missions/manager.server.ts:1560 (only liveOnce call site), :1588 (step read without liveOnce), :1647-1660 (skill branch passes oneTimeAction from raw approvedOnce), :2135 (device skill refusal), ~3870-3880 (askPermission does not clear approvedOnce), ~4102-4106 (allow_batch setStep keeps approvedOnce), src/lib/bunny-missions/capabilities/bus.server.ts:187 and :318. Status: traced from code; NOT executed as a probe (no probe was run). Capability steps are NOT affected because capabilityRequest's liveOnce clears a CONSUMED grant (onceInvalidity returns the lifecycle state first). Agent-mode missions are largely shielded by reviewedFilesystemOnce's !lifecycle check, but only for lifting a violation, not for standing consent.
verified.repair: Clear or refuse CONSUMED/withdrawn one-time grants in the skill branch: apply liveOnce(step) before building skills.run options (or pass oneTimeAction only when onceInvalidity is null). Also have respond(allow_batch) and any setStep to ready that does not replace approvedOnce clear the stale grant (or let setStep stamp WITHDRAWN on it), so a batch answer never re-arms a consumed write grant.

votes.reasoning:
Traced against the working tree (no probe executed; no repo edits, no git state changes). The finding holds on every hop:

1. Admission stamps but does not clear. bus.server.ts:318 calls this.onceAdmitted only when oneTimeAction === action. manager.server.ts:198-203 implements onceAdmitted as a lifecycle stamp (CONSUMED) and never touches step.approvedOnce.

2. Re-run reads the raw step. runDeterministic reads `let step = this.store.step(stepId)` (manager.server.ts:1588). liveOnce is only called in capabilityRequest (line 1560), so the skill branch never consults onceInvalidity, which would have returned the CONSUMED state (line 2471-2499).

3. Skill branch forwards the stale grant. manager.server.ts:1655 passes oneTimeAction: step.approvedOnce?.action ?? null. skills.server.ts:80-90 loops over every skill step from index 0 on each run and calls bus.request with the same request object, so the filesystem.write is re-issued on re-run.

4. Decide allows it without asking. bus.server.ts:187 sets oneTime when oneTimeAction === action, and authorization.server.ts:392 returns allow before any batch or envelope check. The mitigations (remoteMutationHeld, remoteReviewFor, desktopExecutionConflict) only apply to remote actors or desktop conflicts, not this plain workstation case.

5. The approvedOnce survives the allow_batch path. askPermission's setStep (manager.server.ts:3888) and the allow_batch setStep (line 4110) do not include an approvedOnce key, so no WITHDRAWN stamp fires and the field persists. The only clearing paths are retry (4347), stop (4268), completion (3622) and restart/scope changes, none of which the repro hits. allow_once on the terminal.exec ask would replace the grant (line 4187), so the revival requires the allow_batch answer as stated.

The one-time grant is therefore re-admitted within the same step after CONSUMED, which breaks the stated at-most-one-admission invariant. Impact is bounded: the replayed write uses the skill's fixed params and is only reachable via a workstation allow_batch on a later skill step, so it can silently overwrite a file the user changed since the original approval. Severity MEDIUM is appropriate.</reasoning>
<parameter name="severityIfReal">MEDIUM

Not refuted: the code path is real and matches the trace. (1) skills.server.ts:90 restarts the whole skill from index 0 on every runDeterministic call, so a re-run after an allow_batch on terminal.exec repeats filesystem.write. (2) manager.server.ts:1655 passes oneTimeAction from raw step.approvedOnce (no liveOnce call on this branch; liveOnce only at :1560). (3) respond() at ~4102-4106 sets state ready without touching approvedOnce, and the setStep WITHDRAWN check at :518 only fires when the approvedOnce key is in the patch, so W survives. (4) authorization.server.ts:392 returns allow for context.oneTime before any consumed-state check, and bus.server.ts:187 sets oneTime from oneTimeAction. So a CONSUMED grant does admit a second execution in the same step. Refutation attempts that failed: device answers are refused for skill steps (manager.server.ts:2135), and allow_batch is offered for skill plans (batchOfferFor ~3753). Impact is narrower than the finding suggests. filesystem.write (local.server.ts:108-112) defaults overwrite to false, so a re-run that creates a new file fails closed with "already exists" and nothing is written. The re-run does write only when the skill sets overwrite:true. In that case it rewrites identical bytes to the approved path, but it would also clobber any change made to that file between the approval and the re-run, without a fresh prompt. That is a real but narrow authority gap, so LOW rather than MEDIUM. Not executed as a live probe; static trace only. The skill-restart-from-zero behavior that re-runs earlier side effects is a broader pre-existing design issue, not specific to this grant. Consider MEDIUM only if shipped skills use overwrite:true on a step that runs before an ask.
